newsitem.title: USA: Ft. Devens, Mass. $200 mln project makes progress.
newsitem.headline: Ft. Devens, Mass. $200 mln project makes progress.

text.p: The redevelopment of Fort Devens received a needed shot in the arm Monday when the Committee on Long Term Debt and Capital Expenditures approved $200 million for renovations to the former Army base, State House News Service reported.

The downsizing and subsequent closure last year of the 4,500-square acre base in Ayer cost the central Massachusetts region thousands of jobs, and affected ancillary businesses as well. But plans have been in the making for most of the decade to reinvent the area as a commerce center. Already, 32 projects have been approved for the site, totaling 1,300 permanent jobs. Further, the federal government has committed four projects costing $114 million that will bring 1,200 jobs to Devens.

But the Massachusetts Development Finance Agency - the state agency coordinating the project - has insisted that it needs $200 million promised by the Legislature in 1993 legislation, but never actually funded.

Michael Hogan, MDFA's executive director, said his agency has spent more than $30 million on the Devens project, expecting the state would follow through with the money. However, Hogan now fears that MDFA will have less than $7 million by the end of Fiscal Year 1997, jeopardizing its projects in other parts of the state.

"We've been advancing funds in good faith," Hogan said. He said MDFA has about $125 million in assets, and likes to keep about 10 percent of that in cash reserves. "If this does not pass, it not only hurts Devens, but it would limit our ability to finance other projects as well," he said.

Hogan said increased tax revenue for the state will enable the bond, which will total $263 million with interest and other costs, to be retired in 2011. And, he added, the development project will create an $871 million profit for the state in 2035.

Hogan was asked the Devens project will pay operating costs at the time the original debt is retired. He said three revenue streams will be in place within the next 14 years: local property taxes; profits from the selling of utilities such as natural gas, electricity, water, and wastewater treatment; and the leasing of buildings.
The bill now goes to the House Ways and Means Committee.
